nameStory: The "velvetleaf" part of this blueberry's name comes from the soft, fuzzy texture of its leaves, which feel distinctly different from the smooth leaves of most other blueberries. When you gently stroke the underside of a leaf, it feels like touching velvet fabric. This tactile quality makes it one of the easiest blueberries to identify by touch alone.
description: Velvetleaf blueberry is a low-growing shrub that typically reaches 1-3 feet tall, making it shorter than highbush blueberries but similar in height to lowbush varieties. What sets it apart is its distinctively soft, velvety leaves that feel fuzzy to the touch. Like other blueberries, it produces small, bell-shaped white or pinkish flowers in spring, followed by edible blue berries in summer. This hardy northern species is well-adapted to cooler climates and acidic soils.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves feel soft and velvety, especially on the underside, due to fine hairs covering the surface. They're oval-shaped with pointed tips and have a fuzzy texture that's immediately noticeable when you touch them.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, bell-shaped flowers hang in clusters, typically white to pale pink in color. They dangle downward like tiny lanterns and appear in late spring to early summer.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue berries with a whitish bloom (waxy coating) ripen in mid to late summer. The berries are sweet but can have a slightly tart or 'sour' taste, earning it the nickname 'sourtop blueberry.'

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading colonies 1-3 feet tall through underground runners. The shrubs often grow in patches rather than as isolated individual plants.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are often reddish-brown and may have a slightly fuzzy texture. Older stems develop a gray-brown bark that's relatively smooth.

habitat: Velvetleaf blueberry thrives in acidic, well-drained soils in cooler regions of New England, particularly at higher elevations and in northern areas. You'll often find it in open woodlands, forest edges, clearings, and areas that have been disturbed by logging or fire. It's commonly associated with other heath family plants like other blueberries, huckleberries, and mountain laurel.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic velvety texture, and small bell-shaped white to pink flowers appear in late spring, typically May to early June.
seasonality.summer: Dark blue berries ripen from mid-July through August, and the velvety leaves are at their most distinctive for identification purposes.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of orange, red, and purple before dropping, creating spectacular autumn color displays.
seasonality.winter: The bare, reddish-brown twigs and low branching pattern help identify the shrub, along with any persistent dried berries from the previous season.

funFact: Despite being called 'sourtop blueberry,' the berries actually become sweeter after the first frost, as the cold temperatures convert starches to sugars - making late-season picking a treat for both humans and wildlife preparing for winter.
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with lowbush blueberry, but the velvet test is foolproof - lowbush blueberry leaves are smooth and hairless, while velvetleaf blueberry leaves feel distinctly fuzzy. Memory trick: 'Velvet equals velvety leaves!'
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called 'Canadian blueberry' because it's more common in northern regions and extends well into Canada, representing the cold-hardy end of the blueberry spectrum. The multiple common names (velvetleaf huckleberry, sourtop blueberry, common blueberry) can cause confusion, but they all refer to the same fuzzy-leaved species.
compareHints: Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves. It's shorter than highbush blueberry but grows in similar colonies to lowbush blueberry. The velvety leaf texture is your instant identification key, setting it apart from all other Vaccinium species in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter.
Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries.
Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves.
Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants.

Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
